#3606. Martin McDonagh Calls Sam Rockwell “One of the Best Actors of His Generation, If Not the Best”

Director Martin McDonagh has become as well-known for making memorable films as he is for writing the complex male friendships within them.

"I like mining down into the sensitivity that I think a lot of male relationships do have, but aren't as – especially in American films – explored sensitively," he said about the subject during a panel conversation at the inaugural Vanity Fair Screening Room at LACMA on Friday. "It's not just a buddy film, and it's not a romance, and it's not just about cool CIA guys," McDonagh continued. “It's sort of the opposite in other ways. And that I think is interesting to explore because I think my male relationships are that way. They can be sensitive and sad and happy and all the things that a female relationship can be. So I think that's why I keep coming back to it.”

The conversation, which featured McDonagh and the film’s stars John Malkovich and Mariana di Girolamo, was moderated by VF's Senior Hollywood Correspondent Rebecca Ford following an exclusive screening of their new film, Wild Horse Nine. The acclaimed dark comedy follows two CIA agents (Malkovich and Sam Rockwell) who are not only behind the plan to overthrow the Chilean government in 1973, but have also had a hand in several other significant historical moments in the US and abroad.

Maria di Girolamo, John Malkovich and Martin McDonagh, in conversation with Rebecca Ford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on Friday, November 13, 2026.

Malkovich and Rockwell's characters engage in pithy, often hilarious banter throughout the film, and their onscreen chemistry is a highlight.

John Malkovich at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

"I love Sam," said Malkovich. “I knew him a bit socially before this, but I'd worked with him once before, which was a great pleasure on a film called A Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. He's like a kind of expert trainer at SeaWorld who can get the whales and the sharks and the dolphins to show things in exchange for a fish. And Sam is a great student of acting. He is a great student of film and of theater, and he's great fun, very hardworking, and just an ideal colleague. I couldn't imagine a better colleague than Sam and I've had some excellent colleagues.”

"He's one of the best actors of his generation, if not the best," adds McDonagh of Rockwell. "He's always surprising, always dangerous, always sensitive, always smart, always coming up with new stuff. And I think there's a danger to him that's lovely to write for. We always hope the characters will always be surprising, and with Sam's voice in the head, that really helps."

Mariana di Girolamo at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

For rising star Mariana di Girolamo, a Chilean actress making her English language movie debut with Wild Horse Nine, she was excited and only slightly intimidated to be a part of the cast.

"It was quite a challenge to perform for the first time in English," she said. "I prepared myself with a coach and we rehearsed with John, Sam and Parker [Posey] and Ailin [Salas] in a public theater in New York where I heard the script for the first time. That was amazing for me, for us." di Girolamo, who is very familiar with the fraught period of Chilean history depicted in the film, said she appreciated how McDonagh put it all in context. "It was my first time approaching that period of time in this way with this very beautiful dark humor. I was laughing about these things and feeling empathy with these CIA agents that committed a lot of horrific, horrific things. I've never read something like that, and the arc of my character is so beautiful, unique, I really wanted to be part of this."

Martin McDonagh at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair's Screening Room pairs this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that includes post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. The invitation-only events are welcoming an audience from the worlds of film, fashion, culture, politics, media, and tech, much like the magazine itself. VF editor Daniel Kile introduced the first screening, welcoming the audience to the Steve Tisch Theater at LACMA, which is not yet open to the public.

Maria di Girolamo, John Malkovich and Martin McDonagh, in conversation with Rebecca Ford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on Friday, November 13, 2026.

Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

#3604. UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is more worried "about the amount of time" people will spend on GTA 6 than the game's violent content

"I remember in my childhood playing Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter. I didn't hit anybody after playing those games."

Leader of the UK Conservative Party (and former Mortal Kombat player) Kemi Badenoch is more worried about the amount of time people will spend playing GTA 6 rather than the game itself.

Every new Grand Theft Auto game invites some amount of controversy over its in-game violence or depictions of sex and drugs - from San Andreas' raunchy Hot Coffee mini-game to GTA 5's graphic torture scene. Ahead of GTA 6's release this week, the Tory leader downplayed those fears.

"I would be more worried about the amount of time people were spending on a game than the game specifically. I remember in my childhood playing Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter. I didn't hit anybody after playing those games," Badenoch said in a news conference shared by Sky News (good spot, IGN).

While Badenoch's stance might be surprising for the normally right-wing UK political party, she did still worry over children who might play GTA 6 for too long. There are probably far worse ways for kids to spend their time than engaging with a long-form story like GTA 6's, though, especially in an era with endless amounts of 10-second clips to mindlessly scroll past and declining funding into youth programs.

"I haven't played Grand Theft Auto, I know people are worried about the game content. At the same time, I'd be more worried about a kid who played it all day, who was in their bedroom all day, than one who spends half an hour on it and then went out and did something else. They are two different things," Badenoch added.

GTA 6's release is imminent and is expected to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time. One analyst even suggested GTA 6 could make over $2bn in its opening weekend - that's handily more money than Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey made during its entire run in cinemas, for context.

If you'd like to reminisce a bit before the long-awaited game finally hits, you can check out our favourite Grand Theft Auto pieces Eurogamer's published over the years.

We've said previously that, for better or worse, the third-person sci-fi RPG Exodus looks a lot like Mass Effect. It's a characterization that developer Archetype Entertainment isn't shying away from—in fact, it seems to be actively embracing it with the reveal of the game's female protagonist, who they refer to as Femjun.

I kid you not, this is not a name I've cooked up or run across on social media. It's right there on the Exodus website: "Meet Femjun! You’ve been waiting to see FemJun, and today we’re happy to say she’s finally here."

Femjun is a very direct reference to Femshep, the female version of Commander Shepard in BioWare's Mass Effect trilogy. While the male version was effectively the default playable character through the first two games, BioWare took steps to put them on equal footing for Mass Effect 3. That effort included a vote to let fans decide the character's official face, which was subsequently used on alternate or inside covers of Mass Effect 3 packaging.

Voiced by Jennifer Hale, Femshep became so popular that when BioWare dropped the Mass Effect Legendary Edition trailer, it was she who appeared most prominently.

So, back to Exodus: Fenjum will be portrayed by Carina Conti, who's appeared in television shows including Tracker, Good Trouble, All Rise, and Winning Time: The Rise of the Lakers Dynasty. Exodus will be only her second videogame credit, though, following Mafia: The Old Country, in which she portrayed Isabella Torrisi. The male version of Jun will be played by veteran voice actor Stephen Oyoung.

Narrative director Drew Karpyshyn also confirmed that romances in Exodus won't be locked out based on whether you play male or female Jun: "We want to make sure that players can engage in what romances they want if you pursue them."

Exodus is set to launch on April 7, 2027, and will be available for PC on Steam and the Epic Games Store.

#3601. Original GTA 6 leaker pleads guilty to hacking Rockstar Games, years after first revealing Lucia

The 21-year-old responsible for hacking Rockstar Games and leaking in-development GTA 6 footage in 2022 has pleaded guilty to a number of offenses.

The GTA 6 leaker was initially sentenced to an indefinite stay at a hospital due to his severe autism, but was more recently deemed fit for trial and moved to a regular prison earlier this January. On Monday, at the Woolwich Crown Court in South East London, he pleaded guilty to hacking Rockstar Games and a number of other companies, including Uber and EE/BT, in cyber attacks estimated to have caused £10m in damages.

At the time of his Rockstar hack - when he was between the ages of 16 and 17 - the leaker was already under police protection at a Travelodge hotel to keep him from rival hackers he had allegedly stolen Bitcoin from. Somewhat surprisingly, he then managed to hack the multi-billion dollar game maker with nothing but an Amazon Fire Stick, the hotel room's TV and a bluetooth-connected keyboard and mouse.

As the BBC reports, he also managed to break into the developer's Slack channels, before threatening to release the GTA 6 source code if Rockstar failed to contact him within the day. The leaker has yet to be sentenced.

Those 2022 leaks were quite substantial, too, revealing about an hour of unfinished gameplay and clueing the world in on Lucia's existence - the series' first female protagonist in years. Of course, those 2022 leaks shouldn't be confused with 2026's, which saw Cyberleek spill nuggets of nearly finished clips onto the internet, despite Rockstar's best efforts to keep GTA 6 a closely guarded secret.

"We recently suffered a network intrusion in which an unauthorised third-party illegally accessed and downloaded confidential information from our systems, including early development footage for the next Grand Theft Auto," Rockstar said at the time, before it had officially unveiled GTA 6. "At this time we do not anticipate any disruption to our live game services, nor any long-term effect on the development of our ongoing projects. We are extremely disappointed to have any details of our next game shared with you all in this way."

Four years later, GTA 6 is finally around the corner - you're probably already aware considering the marketing frenzy Rockstar's been drumming up.

I can't remember the last time a Saturday Night Live sketch had people talking quite as much as the "Sister" sketch has. Former SNL writer and frequent host John Mulaney returned to host SNL this past weekend, and among the sketches featured was a faux medical ad for "Sister," the ultimate elder care provider for your family. The clip has sparked quite a bit of conversation after humorously raising the topic of daughters -- and in many cases, by proxy, their spouses -- being relied on more often than sons to make themselves available, and oftentimes upend their lives, to care for an aging parent. It's the rare kind of sketch that makes people laugh as much as it makes many want to cry at the truth of it.

It's been interesting to see the comments from fans across social media in response to the sketch, but I also found myself wanting to watch it again, and a few funny things caught my eye when I did.

One subtle detail that I appreciated was the fact that when Mulaney's "Brother" character texts his sister to alert her that "dad fell," we see that the previous text exchanges between the two siblings are bland Happy Birthday messages from brother.

I hate when a movie or TV series shows a text exchange on screen and it's clear there were no previous texts between two people who likely have texted in the past. Not only does the "Sister" SNL sketch avoid that bit of annoyingness, it also uses the previous texts to show us just how much distance exists between these two particular siblings. It's funny and also makes me feel bad -- kind of like the whole sketch does.

Also, I did briefly question why there wasn't a Happy Birthday text from Sister to Brother between the two he'd sent to her (marking a year passing between the two exchanges), then quickly deduced that it's likely because she called him on his birthday, instead of texting.

At the very end of the sketch, I had to pause it to read the captions. As is the case in many pharmaceutical ads, this one wraps up with a nod to the company responsible for the treatment, and then runs through a rapid but alarming list of potential side effects.

If you missed any of this, here's what it says:

This seems like a dry dig at "Brother," lest he forget that the person or people in need of care are presumably the same person/people who brought him into the world and raised him.

As for the side effects, disclaimers and warnings:

Quantities are limited. Sister may break down without warning. Offer void if sister has a good therapist.

It seems fair to warn users that the sister who's being relied on to shoulder most or all of the responsibility of care might occasionally emotionally collapse under the weight of it. And it's also fair to warn users that this "elder care system" won't work on any sister who has the psychological support to help her see through any suggestion or pressure that she should be the sole person responsible for care-giving. Quantities are limited sounds more like a mention for an HSN sale item than it does for medical treatment, but I suppose the messaging really is true for all siblings. I sure am grateful for mine!

This Saturday Night Live sketch has only been up on YouTube for a couple of days and has already amassed more than three million views. It's quickly becoming one of those sketches that makes the round and will likely be talked about and remembered for a long time. You can watch the sketch below, or check out John Mulaney's full episode of SNL with a Peacock subscription.

#3599. Andrew Scott On What Makes Elsinore “So Moving”

Although the emotional core of Elsinore is centered around beloved actor Ian Charleston dealing with terminal illness, its star Andrew Scott says the film has as much heart as it does humor.

“The most singular thing about our film I think is the humor in it,” he said during a panel conversation at the inaugural Vanity Fair Screening Room at LACMA on Friday. “The tragedy in some ways is a little bit like Hamlet itself, but you can't make a film about Ian Charleston without having gags in it. He was incredibly funny. Every person [who knew him] said he was just wickedly funny, and flirtatious, and he was always looking towards the light, and he had a certain degree of courage. So that is something I think that we all share as a sense of humor.”

Andrew Scott, Billie Piper, Stephen Beresford and Rebecca Ford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

Elsinore tells the story of Scottish actor Ian Charleson (Scott) who attempts to perform Hamlet at the National Theatre while secretly living with AIDS. Scott has received early acclaim for his powerful portrayal of Charleson. Before the film began Vanity Fair’s West Coast Editor John Ross warned the audience that "first you're going to laugh, then you're going to cry," while watching Scott’s performance.

“I think … why the film is so moving is because [Charleson’s] not wallowing at any point. He was insanely courageous,” continued Scott. “So that to me was the thing that we were the most

insistent on in some ways. And that's really all down to finding actors who in this extraordinary ensemble have a really terrific sense of humor. And we kind of knew that we could, with the screenplay, get the best actors in the country. And I feel we did.”

The panel conversation featured Scott, costar Billie Piper, and writer Stephen Beresford, moderated by VF's Senior Hollywood Correspondent Rebecca Ford, following an exclusive screening of the film.

Billie Piper at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

For Piper, who plays Charleston's close friend Patsy, she relied heavily on Beresford's script for her prep, as well as information she gleaned from those who actually knew Patsy, and Charleston.

“I've spoken to a few members of the family, their friends, and then I sort of cherry-picked things from people I'd known in the beginning of my career, the louder figures in our industry,” she said. “And then I did my own interpretation and just had a good time. It's a very moving story, but I had a lot of fun playing that part. She's a really joyful character to play, I enjoyed the comedy. And I understand that a lot of her jokes are coming from a place of despair.”

Beresford, who has known Scott for 25 years, said he didn't initially think of his longtime friend for the role, but should have.

“The story of Ian, and Ian's Hamlet [performance] is legendary in the British theater,” he said. “So many people said it was the greatest Hamlet they'd ever seen, and that it had this incredible quality. So I knew about the story, and then it was brought to me actually as an idea by a producer who said, ‘What about writing about Ian Charleston, and what about Andrew playing Ian Charleston?’ And then I just thought, ‘Well, why didn't I have that idea myself five years ago?’ So yeah, that's really how it happened, and I started to research it, the details of the story were so incredible, and so moving.”

Stephen Beresford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026.

Scott, who famously played Hamlet onstage 150 times beginning in 2017, prior to filming Elsinore, closed out the panel conversation by reciting his favorite line from the classic tragedy.

“When Hamlet says the line about the war that was going on—and this was written 400 years ago—it just seems so relevant to what he might have been experiencing at the time, which is: ‘I see the imminent death of 20,000 men who for a fantasy, a trick of fame, go to their graves like beds.’ The idea that that was written 400 years ago, and that he was watching 50 percent of his friends die for no reason and be neglected by governments, and derided by the public. And it was just happening, and happening time and time again.”

Scott continued: “The reason that I love it so much is that when I was doing Hamlet myself, of course I wasn't thinking about the AIDS crisis, but the enduring nature of art, something that was written 400 years ago by Shakespeare, could actually be of use to somebody in 1989 and then be reproduced again in 2026 and be of use. And that idea of art being useful down the lines is so moving to me.”

Vanity Fair's Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci, Elsinore stars Andrew Scott and Billie Piper and writer Stephen Beresford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026.

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room pairs this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that includes post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. The invitation-only events are welcoming an audience from the worlds of film, fashion, culture, politics, media, and tech, much like the magazine itself.

Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

Andrew Scott, Billie Piper, Stephen Beresford and Rebecca Ford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026.

#3598. Star Wars: Galactic Racer is getting much-requested split-screen multiplayer and new mode in 2027

The surprisingly awesome arcade podracing game Star Wars: Galactic Racer is getting split-screen multiplayer next year after loud fan requests, developer Fuse Games has announced.

Split-screen racing comes as part of an entirely new mode called Free Play that'll also allow players to mix and match vehicles, characters, tracks and planets in a galaxy far, far away. So, maybe don't expect to bring friends into the game's vast, pre-existing suite of modes just yet.

"We heard you," the studio wrote on social media. "Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at Fuse Games has been working hard to bring a brand new mode, Free Play, to Star Wars: Galactic Racer. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action."

We’ve heard you! Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at @Fuse_Games has been working hard to bring a brand new mode, Free Play, to STAR WARS: Galactic Racer™. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action.

Galactic Racer already has a pretty good selection of online multiplayer modes, like the 12-player speeder races and 8-player podracing tours, but there's currently no way to play with your mates in the same room.

Chris Donlan loved the thrilling racing game for mixing the best bits of Star Wars and Burnout - Fuse Games does have plenty of old Criterion DNA, mind you. "It's new games, with Roguelite choices and endless unlockables, and it's also old games, with cruel and ingenious courses where everything can be lost in an instant. It's a Galaxy Far, Far Away, and it's also Paradise City," he wrote in Eurogamer's five-star review.

With Galactic Racer and Zero Company under its belt, Lucasfilm Games said it's now "more flexible" about which developers it accepts pitches from. Hopefully, that'll lead to even more interesting games set in Star Wars' ultra flexible world.

#3597. The Games Industry Said Black Lives Matter, Then It Disappeared

Six years ago, the games industry said Black Lives Matter. During the protests nationwide (and beyond) over the police murders of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor, there was no ignoring peopleâs rage and the clear truths that fueled it. The games industry, as well as society, found a mirror held up to itself regarding racism.Â Â

This period reinforced that the North American games sector has always operated under and reflected the social, economic, and political systems of the nation in which it is based. We spoke with a cohort of Black game developers to assess the industryâs responses to 2020, to understand the realities of the industry today in all its contradictions and challenges, and to examine its ongoing relationship with Black professionals.Â

In the midst of the wider racial justice movement of 2020, numerous game companies publicly announced donations to Black organizations, businesses, and efforts against racial injustice. Ubisoft, for instance, donated $100,000 to the NAACP and Black Lives Matter. Square Enix, meanwhile, said at the time that it would contribute $250,000 to the Black Lives Matter organization and other charities.Â

We stand in solidarity with Black team members, players, and the Black community. We are making a $100,000 contribution to the NAACP and Black Lives Matter and encourage those who are able to, to donate. #BlackLivesMatter pic.twitter.com/KpHZCF6VWx

#BlackLivesMatter (1/2) pic.twitter.com/luAbZQWmuQ

While on the surface these gestures may seem like sincere efforts to help address the racial inequities that exist in the United States, they can more honestly be viewed as moves meant to generate good PR, and understandably received criticism as a result. In their book Laundering Black Rage, authors Too Black and Dr. Rasul A. Mowatt offer a frank appraisal of the actions of many U.S. companies at this time.Â Â Â

âHow was the contagious Black Rage provoked by the police officerâs knee on a poor Black manâs neck converted into a benign commodity that could be massively marketed by corporations?â they ask.

Among the companies making such pledges was also EA. The publisher, on a now-deleted page titled “actions-against-racial-injustice,” said it would contribute $1 million to organizations such as the Equal Justice Initiative and the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund. Itâs unknown why that landing page was removed.Â Â

Former EA and Respawn narrative designer Jarory De Jesus believes the decision to remove the post was likely political. The current presidential administration is fiercely anti-DEI, and has taken measures against some businesses that have DEI policies, while threatening to take measures against others.

âIt has to do with the current political environment,â says De Jesus. âIn 2024 and subsequent years, you saw a lot of a shift away from positive outlooks on diversity, towards a more âneutralâ stance. It’s not really a neutral stance; no stance is neutral,â he explains.Â Â

De Jesus juxtaposes EAâs decision to take down the page with the support he received while working at mobile game developer Scopely in 2020, during the height of the protests. The publisher told its staffers that it had allocated a million dollars to support any facing legal issues for engaging in protests. If employees wanted to attend protests, they would be supported. This support wasnât something the narrative writer felt while at EA.

Still, the years werenât all bad as the industry preached more diversity and equality. De Jesus also felt that supportive sentiment was present during his time at Respawn Entertainment. He helped with the efforts of the companyâs DEI board while concurrently, the Apex Legends team was working on trans hero Catalyst.Â

Eventually, however, the industry-wide support that had started in 2020 stopped. Nearly everyone I spoke to noted that any serious efforts initiated during that period had mostly wound down or been shut down three years later.Â

Parallel with this, the Supreme Court effectively prohibited affirmative action in 2023. Additionally, in 2023, a wave of anti-trans laws was passed across the country. This effectively gave the current presidential administration a runway to go after firms and programs it believed were antithetical to American values.Â

De Jesus says, âItâs really unfortunate because we were making a lot of progress, you know, at least in terms of representation in games. It’s not [as if] we’re out here making technology that’s going to redefine someone’s livelihood. We are going to maybe help people identify and find the right way to express themselves.âÂ

Meanwhile, among the changes that have taken place over the years, layoffs and studio closures have become as commonplace as game releases. It must be understood that the broader layoffs affecting millions in America are a response to a combination of factors including real-world market forces, AI adoption/implementation, U.S. geopolitical warfare, inflation, tariffs, and so forth.

De Jesus reflects on the years of widespread layoffs in the games industry and what they have meant for him. He says, âIt pains me to see people who I know are clearly talented, clearly driven, hardworking, inspired individuals that just get laid off without any noticeâ¦I think the biggest [loss for those who remain] is the cultural stuff. When you lose pillars of your community within your company, that can be devastating. Because, especially at the AAA level, it allows you to reshape a culture into something more homogeneous, safe, and less organic.âÂ

The game writer adds, âThe other thing that I think is worth mentioning isâ¦you’re going to see a lot more smaller indie and AA studios popping up from those same talented creative professionals that were let go.â

The year of racial justice uprisings was also an interesting time for nonprofits to navigate as donations and contributions came in, according to Catt Small, executive director of Game Devs of Color, Inc (GDoC).Â

Small explains, âI think we were really grateful for being given the funding that we could then route to people who needed it. [It] was something that was really meaningful for us. But because of what it was tied to at the same time, I think we all felt internally that this was temporary. This was something that was tied to a moment, and it was possible that the moment was not going to result in longer-term consistent structural change. While we want that to happen and are working toward giving game developers of color the power to be able to create that long-term change where they can support themselves and tell the stories they want to tellâ¦while we want that to happen and are working at that, we had a strong feeling that for primarily white institutions, this was a temporary optical presentation.â

But while Small is well aware that gaming companies may have their own motivations for these initiatives, sheâs also frank about the fact that GDoC wants to achieve its mission, which is to amplify the creative power of people of color in video games. This effort requires receiving help from all interested parties, even if they are largely interested in a good one-off PR story.

Expanding on her point, the executive director says, âAt large, especially primarily white institutions, they’re mostly thinking about things on a quarterly basis. That’s part of it; the way that capitalism is structured encourages people to think about things in terms of what will be perceived in that particular moment.â

The occasional donation, however, is far from sufficient to address the daily material conditions of local Black communities.

While sheâs been a game maker for 14 years, the GDoC executive director says that especially now, she doesnât fully trust the games sector to provide her with a livelihood.Â

She explains, âIt is really challenging as an industry. Because the reality is that games are these interactive experiences that are very based on feelings. They touch people emotionally, which can require a lot of work and is very creative, which is what draws me to it. At the same time, we’re trying to [create these works within] capitalism, which is inherently about what is the quickest way that we can extract money from people. There’s a tension there.âÂ

She acknowledges that marginalized people still need material help. This means having access to resources, mentorship, and opportunities for connection, which GDoC regularly offers.Â

Small explains, âAccess to capital is what matters most, for most people; mentorship and relationships are also incredibly valuable, but the difference between somebody actually building that idea that becomes the next major hit and not doing that is money.â

There was a brief window of what could be called âwe understand your problems, Black people.â However, that led to a larger, reactionary formation of racist, sexist, and homophobic antagonism toward games and developers from a vocal minority. Gamergate 2.0, while lacking the headline-grabbing scale of the original, nonetheless permeated online culture as an effective misinformation and disinformation campaign, much to Smallâs chagrin.Â

She explains, âI think there’s a narrative that Black people have been in power this whole time and are forcing all of these game companies to put stories that they care about in placeâ¦It has been over a decade of just people, game devs of color, women, queer people, just being harassed constantly.Â

âI’ve had friends and great people that I know who had to lock down their social media, or they’ve been laid off from companies in part because of something that was taken out of context.â

Again, those making games and working in the business of games canât escape or ignore reality, as EA alum and programmer Kat Barkwell highlights in her account of beginning work in the sector. Before working in Edmonton, Alberta, her father cautioned her about the cityâs deep issues of systemic racism. But it also happens to be a game development hub.

Starting out at BioWare developing Anthem, the programmer first joined a womenâs employee resource group (ERG). However, she left the group, citing its nearly-all-white composition, which didnât align with her values. She eventually found a better fit in the BEAT (Black EA Team) ERG.

Eventually, Covid-19-era remote work led to a positive turn in her career, as she had her first Black manager.Â

â[The] advice I got from well-meaning managers before just wouldn’t apply to me because I’m a programmer, I’m quiet, I’m introverted. [Theyâd tell me to] keep my head down, do good work, âpeople are going to see that.â And then my [first Black] manager [said], âThey think you’re lazy. If you don’t talk about what you’re doing all the time, they’re going to think you’re lazyâ¦You gotta show it to them.â And that made a big difference in my career,â the programmer explains.

Also, following the industryâs broader acknowledgment of racial issues, EA leadership became receptive to suggestions of support for causes such as GDoC and local organizations that assist marginalized game creators and future developers. Barkwell dedicated time to those efforts to make the industry more inclusive.

But when the expiration date for so-called racial solidarity came, emails requesting contributions were eventually ignored. The BioWare alum says the shift revealed that the attention paid to these issues by EA and other corporations had been shallow from the beginning.Â

Working through this and seeing layoffs hit EA led Barkwell to become increasingly frustrated with the industry. These frustrations, along with her experiences, served as the basis for an analytical presentation she gave for GDoC last year.

âHow do you not be pissed all the time working in this industry? I’m filled with rage all the time, and I don’t have anywhere to put it, cause I’m mad and it sucks, and I tell people âhey, that’s super,ââ the programmer explains.Â

Barkwell continues, presenting a socio-political analysis that gets to the heart of the matter by examining societyâs overall reaction to 2020.

She says, âYou’re here, and you want more people hereâ¦I’m trying to do everything I can to make sure it’s hospitable. They’re happy to spend you as a token and currency. When it’s the right time for it, and you know, a token is there to be spent. Then once it’s spent, that’s it. So you can kick and scream about it. I guess that’s how I felt about it, bad, yeah, but not surprised at the same time too. Of course, that’s what they always do, right?â

After working on 2025âs Skate., the programmer made the choice to leave AAA game development for a better work environment, a better culture, and peace of mind.Â

2020 can also be understood as a time when the issues that Black people in games had been observing and speaking about for years became, however briefly, impossible for others to ignore.Â  Analyzing these observations and conditions has been a part of the career of some game developers, such as Tanya DePass. The conversations echoed the work she began when establishing the non-profit I Need Diverse Games in 2016.Â

â[The 2020 support for Black folks] felt basically [like] taking the guilt, the anger about what was going on in the industry and what was driving many of us outâa lot of femmes out, a lot of queer folks out, a lot of trans folks out, the forces that were trying to get rid of us, compounding that with, hey, you know what, you could do something about this,â she says.

Looking back, she recognizes 2020 and the few years afterwards as a golden era. She was able to get work contracts, share contracts with others, and offer referrals for projects.Â

However, the industry has since contracted due to economic shifts and waves of job cuts. DePass cites the closure of Cliffhanger Games, the cancellation of its Black Panther project, the shuttering of Monolith Productions, and the sunsetting of its Wonder Woman game as particularly damning.Â

Additionally, she says that this targeting of games featuring Black and female heroes for cancellation lends a false legitimacy to the online hate mob against diversity, allowing them to feel correct in their belief that “true gamers” aren’t interested in games that prominently feature such characters. However, the writer emphasizes that paying attention to this hateful minority is not important to the business of game-making.

âThese are the people who claim they love games, but don’t want everyone to access themâ¦We saw Gamergate try to rise up again a couple of years ago. Y’all don’t have anything better to do? Wait, you don’t,â she says.

Returning to the subject of job loss, DePass notes that the industry has become a rat race for employment. She adds that requiring employees to move to expensive cities for roles doesnât make sense, either, when the possibility of layoffs hangs over peopleâs heads like the Sword of Damocles. Making matters worse, recent reports reveal that Black applicants must also navigate biased technology when job hunting.

Whatâs also top of mind, she explains, is that these waves of layoffs are resulting in a brain drain for the games industry. In totality, DePass says, âthe state of the industry is fucked up.â

She refers to the GDC State of the Industry report, which surveys game developers in the U.S. to get a sense of the industryâs racial and ethnic composition.

DePass notes that 30 percent of those surveyed identified as queer. Getting more granular with the data, the industry is 64-percent men and 67-percent white. A majority of people working in the industry fall between the ages of 25 and 44. DePass draws particular attention to the stat line for Black game developers, who make up 5 percent of the reported total.

âIn the 12 years since I’ve been doing this work, still the majority is 67-percent white dudes, and we are only 5 percent. That has only gone up 2 percent since I started doing this work. The first year I looked at one of these, we were only 3 percent of the developers that were self-reported in the developer satisfaction survey, which is the industry-standard [source of data],â she explains.

Still, DePass acknowledges that there are more Black folks in gaming now than there were in the past. She highlights the Black in Gaming Awards, for example. However, she cautions that the industry is still functionally exclusionary. For example, GDC is recognized as a good networking event. However, it comes with a high price tag, prohibitively high for many working-class people. And even if people are able to get tickets to the show, theyâll still need to obtain air travel and a hotel stay in, in one of the most economically antagonistic cities in the US.

Senior character artist Del Walker has done a series of YouTube videos in which he discusses his experiences in game development and the multifaceted economic precarities that game makers face.

In one episode, Walker says, âMy issue is that the cost of living is now untenable for most peopleâ¦Capitalism is now at its threshold moment where I need to figure out how to survive the tidal wave. Simply put, the growing costs of development and the standard cost of living, particularly in California where the majority of the U.S. games industry operates, result in a reality where it’s not possible to make anything without insane risk.Â

âYou have people on payroll at a studio, you need to pay them the cost of what it is to be in a city. That’s where all the talent is, and no one’s really addressing why it costs so much and is so high-riskâ¦ because no one has solved the problem that houses shouldn’t cost millions. I’m looking at it more from the point of view that this is not getting better; in fact, it’s accelerating, it’s getting worse,â he adds.

When asked specifically whether relocating the industry to lower-cost areas in the U.S. would be a solution, he replies, âYou’re not really changing the source of the sickness if you keep saying, well, everyone just needs to just not be in California.âÂ

âOK, cool. So do we just play the same game in Atlanta? Is this what we do? We find a hub, and then we just burn it out and make it untenable to live there, and then say, hey, everyone, we’re moving to South Carolina, what’s the game?â¦ It’s seeing the plague is spreading, and you just move north? And that’s your answer every 15 years?â

Walker cites Matthew Ballâs State of the Industry Report to illustrate how the industry got to where it is today. Six years ago, with covid-19 keeping people indoors, the gaming industry received a revenue boost it hasnât seen since. This resulted in companies becoming ambitious (some would say misguided) as they expanded their employee numbers, investments, and merger and acquisition activityâarguably beyond their scope.

Walker explains, âThe largest problem is definitely still a greed problem, because you had in 2020, when everyone got locked into COVID, and everyone was trying to figure out their shareholder valueâ¦You have a harder fall when you realize that the numbers you were hiring on were predicated on temporary situations or kind of finessed.âÂ

He continues, âBut where it fell down is larger than it was pre-pandemic, so the games industry is growing, it just should have never grown that fast. And there was a lot of hurt and pain caused by exploding that quickly. There are a few other things that are happening there as well, because you also have companies that went from small to medium, and you had medium companies that went from medium to enormous.â

To his point, the chase for 2020âs revenue, the changing economy, fewer investments in games, and other such factors have largely led to job losses and studio closures.Â

Where do these economic shifts leave the Black proletariat? Historically and presently, data supports the fact that when the economy is facing a bad time, Black workers across industries are often the first to be laid off.Â Â

Walker also said that the current state of the industry calls for more game professionals who are generalists rather than specialists. He argues that most current job listings in the games industry are effectively âasking for Jesus to apply.âÂ

The summer of 2020 also created conditions in which firms could gain unique institutional insights. Sweet Baby Inc. co-founder and CEO Kim Belair explains that the narrative and consultancy firm was, in part, able to observe how corporations were approaching the âracial reckoningâ matter while working on game projects.

â[Corporations] did not want to get left behind, and I think a lot of money was put [into appearing to support] a lot of folks’ current games industry careers. Money started to show up behind some of these promises. I think it was misleading for some, an opportunity for others, and a kind of true deception for more people.âÂ

The Sweet Baby CEO recalls an observation she made while working on portfolio reviews for Black and marginalized writers, offering feedback in an effort to help them improve their chances of finding work. Belair explains, âThese portfolio reviews, while very kind and very important to the betterment of our craftâ¦[were] not in any way addressing the actual problem. Because if we’re going to be honest, our industry is racist, sexist, and homophobic. What we’re essentially dealing with is that the marginalized people aren’t good enough.â

The period also provided firsthand insight into how game studios can overcome hurdles as they build out their casts. She uses the example of working with Sony Santa Monica on God of War Ragnarok. Following the reveal of Angrboda, who is a young Black girl, racists online were rather vocal about her inclusion.Â Â

âWe got two different emails from Santa Monica going, hey, could you guys come in and talk to us, and how can we learn more?â¦It was because there were very few people discussing the intersection of art and politics for the use of this conversation.âÂ

Belair continues, âOften, the most important expression of both art and politics is at their confluence. That is the discourse we’ve primarily lost in the past few years. It’s not just about wanting to see a Black person in this video game, but we want them written by whoever and we want it told by whoever.âÂ

The CEO notes that not only did the so-called support for Black people expire by 2023, but companies became unwilling to openly defend their creative choices in their more diverse and inclusive games. This created a faÃ§ade in which businesses sought to increase revenue by appearing progressive to a wider consumer base in their gaming projects, while simultaneously betraying those principles by staying silent when more racist and reactionary members of the gaming community criticized them.

Of note, Sweet Baby has drawn immense amounts of harassment and hostility from reactionary gamers who object to what they see as the “forcing” of diverse characters and identities into games. Belair herself, a Black woman, was made the face of a massive hate campaign targeting her narrative and consultancy firm. This happened shortly after the games industry said that it cared about the racial injustice that Black people face.

Still, despite all the hostility directed right at her and her firm, she says, âThe most harmful part of what happened to us is not just about us. It expands to everybody. We allowed studios to get away with saying nothing about the things they make. I think that doesn’t negatively affect Sweet Baby; that negatively affects any marginalized person, and frankly, non-marginalized people who want to say something within these spaces.â

And despite the hate campaign, Sweet Baby continues to get jobs because the industry recognizes the quality of its work. This has allowed Belair to make some interesting revelations regarding game development. When it comes to storytelling and characterization, the games industry, she says, is particularly protective of depictions of cops.

Belair explains, âI’ve been in 1,000 rooms talking about criticism, sensitivity, risks, all these ideas, and I can tell you that the most protected group in video games is cops by a wide margin. You cannot say anything about them. You cannot allude to the idea that the institution may be corruptâ¦If we show a bad one, make sure you show a good one.â

Yes, the police, the same institution responsible for the murders of Breonna Taylor, George Floyd, and countless others. The same institution that has slave-catcher origins. The same institution that received more funding post-2020. The same institution that has a very low rate of nationwide crime prevention. The same institution that has a city built for it in Atlanta so it may surveil its Black population.Â

Kotaku alum and narrative designer Evan Narcisse notes that thereâs a real dichotomy between working in games and dealing with real life.

He expresses concern that the Supreme Court is doing away with the last vestiges of the Voting Rights Act.Â

Back in 2020 and now, his focus remains on material conditions. âI think one of the things that happened in 2020 was that we saw a huge uptick in terms of lip service and vocal support in terms of inclusivity in video games,â he says. âThere were initiatives to hire more people, to mentor more people, that kind of thing. But I’ll say that even then, I was dubious. The Black squares, what does that do for us, as Black people? The signs, painting streets with Black Lives Matter, and these are all surface-level demonstrations. You know, akin to Nancy Pelosi and them kneeling in kente cloth scarves in DC. It’s a gesture. It’s not something that materially changes circumstances for the people that they say they want to support.â

To his point, in a Pew Research report, five years after the murder of George Floyd, most respondents say that âthe increased focus on race and racial inequality after Floydâs killingâ didnât lead to an improvement in the lives of Black people. The social, economic, and political systems that keep Black people and many others oppressed are still alive and well.Â

Now, while some games may look more diverse and inclusive, Narcisse still has questions about whoâs on the development staff. âThis has always been super important to meâ¦who’s behind the scenes working on these projects, who’s making these games, especially the ones that want to traffic in any kind of Black cultural representation?âÂ

Questioning companies’ recruitment and retention pipelines, the game writer asks why there arenât Black game developers who are recognizable industry figures. âWe can debate auteurism all we want, but there hasnât been a Black auteur in video gamesâ¦There’s no Spike Lee in video games. There’s no Ryan Coogler. There are no equivalents to those kinds of names in this industry. It’s because what it takes to sustain a career in video games has always been a matter of socio-cultural alignment that seemingly is not inviting to us.â

Narcisse believes that the industry has barely scratched the surface of what a Black video game is, something he wrote about years ago. He emphasizes that titles can not only reflect stereotypes but also express cultural values unique to the community. He points to the release of Nyamakop’s Relooted as a good recent example.

He notes that throughout his career, heâs often been the only Black narrative designer on projects. Most recently, heâs been working at Brass Lion Entertainment, which is currently developing the game Wu-Tang: Rise of the Deceiver. âThis is a team whose stated purpose is to expand the ranks of Black, Brown, and marginalized game developers,â he says, noting that his tenure there marks the first time in his career that heâs held the title of senior writer on a project.

His assessment of the games industry is heavily influenced by current economic conditions, and the longevity of his career and that of other Black game professionals remains a constant question. âThe New York Times had an article on Black filmmakers such as Julie Dash (Daughters of the Dust) and Kasi Lemmons (The Caveman’s Valentine). These were all movies I saw in college. [I thought] we might be out here doing this thing in real numbers, and all those careers disappear within five, seven, 10 years. That’s always been the boogeyman over my shoulder. Whatever shot I have as a creative professional, there’s a clock on that shit. I don’t know when it’s going to be time’s up for me.â

While things have changed quite a bit in six years, Black Voices in Gaming (BViG) director and career developer Justin Woodward says that the mission statement of the organization, which was founded in response to racial inequity in the gaming space, remains the same.Â

Woodward explains, âThe number one thing is to create opportunities for developers to get funds. Either through our grant process or through various partners, publishers, investors…that’s been the staple from the beginning. Black Voices in Gaming helps to represent underserved developers, especially in the entrepreneurial space.â

Thatâs easier said than done, though, and he says that due to a combination of factors including the current presidential administration, widespread industry layoffs, and a pullback in gaming investments, the organizationâs mission has only become harder to maintain.Â

BViG adds that the U.S., unlike other countries, doesnât have programs or provide government assistance to fund games despite the industry’s size. He highlights that venture capital is now focused on tech, AI, and whatever the latest hype is, and notes that venture capital investment is something of an old boys’ club as well.Â

Still, Woodward says that he and the team had faith that their efforts were proving fruitful after the positive reception of its first showcase. It has now become a regular entry in the assortment of gaming showcases that occur each year. Among the actions Woodward has taken, he served as the head of the Black Game Developer Fund at Humble Bundle, which distributed $1 million a year to Black game makers.

Woodward adds that BViG’s work has also helped support the launch of newer efforts, such as Destinee Clevelandâs Dames 4 Games. Dames 4 Games focuses on elevating the visibility of the games, careers, and networking opportunities of women and femmes.Â

And when support for and investment in initiatives intended to make the games industry more equitable began to dry up, Woodward wasnât surprised. âI’m not surprised by any of it,â he says, âsome of it is just unfortunate. It’s a little disappointing sometimes. It just looked good to front as if you’re helping different causes. Everyone was searching for how [to project] that [they were] helping. So, when that happens, they put a lot of money into it because it’s also additional PR and positive marketing for corporationsâ¦Obviously, when the tides turn, you see that faucet of capital gets turned off for those programs.â

In his analysis, people get let go and programs get shut down because equity is not core to the business of these studios and publishers. Itâs purely transactional, âso you have to roll with the punches.â

He also feels that with everything happening, itâs easy to have a myopic view. Certainly, the games industry is undergoing many changes, and so is society as a whole. However, he wants to focus on the possibilities that lie ahead.

âI have a lot of friends who got laid off. What I would say is, every time this happens, it creates a new renaissance of amazing teams. Although it’s heart-wrenching to see people out of jobs and struggling right now, there’s going to be so much creativity; you’ve heard the adage ânecessity breeds innovation.â People are going to be innovativeâ¦I hope that culturally, they’re able to expand upon their creativity and not just do things that are generic, and push the bar,â he says.

To get a more thorough analytical assessment of the present, we spoke with Adanna Nedd, game developer and author of the Black Game Dev Survey.

While the survey had a relatively small pool of participants, it did provide some further insight into the nature of the field. One of the report’s major topics was industry-wide layoffs, now a normal part of working in the games sector. Neddâs data says that in the past 5 years, â66.1% of Black developers were either directly or knew someone directly impacted by layoffs.â

This is a far cry from how things were six years ago. Explaining how things felt to them in the industry circa 2020, one Black game dev says, âIt felt like a world of possibility was a little bit more on the horizon, people were getting opportunities to talk and work on things. I think we all kind of knew the bubble probably wouldn’t last. But it was nice to think about.â

At their own studio, they felt supported internally by coworkers and peers, and they note that their contributions to a particular title were internally recognized upon the gameâs release. However, acknowledgment of them and other underrepresented team members ceased in the years that followed.Â

Again, a fleeting appearance of dedication to progressive values, quickly cast aside once the moment passes. But this is hardly the greatest frustration the anonymous game dev hasÂ  experienced. Now, they and so many others in the industry are facing the reality of job precarity, which makes for an uneasy working experience.

âIt’s fraught,â they say, âand I feel that you never want to lose your job, especially right now, because there are just so few jobs out there. I can’t speak up on things I may have in the past; I have to cater more to how [management thinks] I should act.Â

âYou always have to kind of do that in a corporate structure. But it’s been more noticeable to me lately, being perceived as aggressive when you’re just trying to do your jobâ¦Oftentimes at the end of day, I’m just exhausted, trying to keep up the proper happy attitude that they want. Sometimes, I just want to put on my headphones and do my job.â Hardly conditions conducive to creative employees doing their best work.

The game maker is also worried about the ballooning costs and production times of developing games, particularly at the mainstream blockbuster level.

They note that the average career in the games industry is roughly five years, and that itâs possible for someone to work in the industry for all that time and not ship a single game.

For an industry that emphasizes shipped projects for career longevity and importance, game credits are elusive. The dev notes that a peer has worked in gaming for close to a decade with multiple canceled projectsâas a result, they have little to show for all that time and effort.Â

They believe this is another reason the industry needs a central union to support professionals and their careers. Unionization efforts have been a boon over the years, but people are still struggling to protect themselves and their peers from fickle CEOs whose fix for their own mismanagement is often mass layoffs.Â

Still, the question of what the games industryâs relationship is with Black game developers remains.Â

Barkwellâs assessment is straightforward: The industryâs relationship with Black game devs is bad. She says that the institution is not interested in change. However, the programmer remains hopeful nonetheless, saying âWhat gives me hope againâ¦with the way the industry is going right now, [is that] no one is better suited to adapt to this sort of stuff than us. If we want to do something, we’ll make it happen. We are the people who set trends. I hope more people go off and do their own thing.â

DePass says she often feels that Black people are treated as a resource rather than as talent. âI wish we could stop having to preface with âI’m a Black game developer,â âI’m a queer game developer,â âI’m a femme developer,â or all three of those. Why can’t I just be a developer? Why can’t I just be a narrative designer?âÂ

However, she emphasizes that Black game professionals need to be in their FUBU era, citing Surgent Studiosâ Tales of Kenzera: Zau and the studioâs founder, Abubakar Salim, as examples.

Sweet Babyâs Belair is very honest and says that the connection between the sector as a whole and Black game makers is âa contentious and cautious relationship right now, and I think that the smartest thing for all parties to do is to again, just be very real about what the deal is.âÂ

Narcisse says that navigating the games industry with his peers is a one-step-at-a-time process. He explains, âIt’s daily, it’s weekly, it’s monthly. I have calls with friends on a recurring basis just so we can get each other’s back and talk about the things that we’re dealing with and experiencing.Â Â

âEvery Black creative professional I know in this field is doing it because they’re a dreamer in the medium and give back, offering their own unique perspectivesâ¦and hopefully produce work that ignites other people.â

When Walker is asked what the games industryâs relationship is with professionals like himself, heâs analytical. âOh man, I’d say there is low trust everywhere now. Very low trust. There are some people who are just full-on jaded. But I’d say theâ¦low trust [is ubiquitous], and that is low trust from professionals and from companies.Â

âI’ve seen people flown from one country to another to join a company and laid off within a week. You know, you are not in my best interest, or you’re telling me I’m doing great on my performance review, and then you lay off all my friends and me suddenly.âÂ

He adds that the way many companies handle hiring has changed, and not for the better. âA studio hires someone based on a reference, and that person ends up being the wrong person, and they have to lay that person off,â the artist says. âNow they double down on low trust, wasted time, and now there’s a level of urgency because no one has cash like they used to.âÂ

Additionally, all the developers I spoke to expressed a concern for creative output. With the current circumstances of the industry, how can they or their peers create work that features new ideas or challenge established norms without fear of losing their jobs?Â

Still, despite the systemic problems, the games industry isnât without altruism and hope. De Jesus notes that being in community with organizations that are dedicated to overlooked populations, such as Black Voices in Gaming, makes the industry feel more supportive and affirming.

There are organizations and people whose work takes a critical look at the American game industryâs capitalist, patriarchal, heteronormative, and white foundations. There are developers who are working on labor movements (and being held accountable). Some game makers, in public solidarity with Palestinians, have supported the BDS movement. When Roe vs. Wade was overruled, some studios and game creators offered support for abortion access.Â Â

However, the contradictions that run through the industry canât be dismissed as mere missteps here and there. The game industry is still one that has been plagued by years of reported and alleged labor issues. There is also a history of game studios having long relationships with the military and defense contractors. EA has just sold itself in a deal involving the current presidentâs son-in-law and Saudi Arabia. And some platform holders have a history of using conflict materials in their product manufacturing.Â

The games industry is not unique in its anti-Black and multifaceted contradictions. Itâs an industry where, in a showcase for new games, a studio reveals that its cast includes the digital zombie of a rapper who was violently murdered 30 years ago, and the crowd just claps and cheers in response. You could also have a Peabody Awardâwinning studio such as Compulsion Games release a title like South of Midnight and still nearly be shuttered a year later.

How many times can we hear executives say theyâre making the âdifficult decisionâ to lay off thousands as if itâs just normal business practice? We live in a society where shareholder value demands constant growth, and the worker be damned.Â

The game industry can pretend that itâs very forward-thinking. However, we must be clear-eyed and push back on institutional mythmaking. Only through real-world analysis, consistent investigation, and understanding the experiences of game developers themselves can we properly assess the industry for what it is across race, gender, and class.

We can organize to challenge the industryâs ills, enjoy the hard work of creative individuals, and reject the social, political, and economic structures it operates under. Games are made by people, and the conditions in which theyâre made are not separate from the reality we all share. Reality demands we not be passive. To invoke the Black authors that everyone supposedly read years ago, we must be collectively dedicated to doing away with these oppressive systems and rebuilding something better to improve our conditions. The starting point in that process was yesterday, the work continues today, and tomorrow we can create that kind of change with the help of our neighborsâespecially the Black ones.

#3596. EA really doesn't want you to delete Madden NFL 27 to make room for GTA 6

"Don't let 210GB get between you and your league."

Assuming you didn't just buy a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S to play Grand Theft Auto 6, your console's limited storage space is likely already strained, meaning tough choices may have to be made to make room for Rockstar's chonky 212GB crime game.

In a move I don't remember seeing before, EA is asking players to spare Madden NFL 27 from the purge to free up console storage space. As spotted by Push Square, a desperate in-game message pops up when you launch the American Football game, pleading with you not to delete it.

The message highlights 17th November as the date of a Madden NFL 27 update, though its styling, wording and choice of background seem to hint at GTA 6.

"Don't delete!" it reads, as shared by Zirksee on X. "[Encrypted Signal] The target is locked. The crew is assembling for a high-stakes run. Await the signal from our insider on 11/17… do not leak this transmission."

EA's language and intention, however, are much clearer in this post on X, which specifically references GTA 6's large file size in a cheeky way, seemingly promoting the same update.

"Don't let 210GB get between you and your league," the post reads, clearly quoting GTA 6's file size.

The update in question is fairly notable, adding a Madden 97 throwback with era-appropriate players, playbooks and what looks to be 16-bit visuals. Though it's obviously not related to GTA 6 in any way, it's easy to see why EA would fear a significant drop in players once Rockstar's game arrives, something other publishers are undoubtedly worried about.

As part of a recent restructuring, EA laid off 400 employees, closed down BioWare, cancelled unannounced projects and revealed a refocusing on its core franchises and biggest monkey-makers. That includes EA Sports, of course, where a team is currently developing a game codenamed Project Gridiron, described as "a social-first open-world experience for our American Football team".

Crystal Dynamics confirmed that eight people have been let go in a "necessary business decision."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Crystal Dynamics has confirmed that eight people have been let go in the latest round of layoffs at the beleaguered Tomb Raider studio.

"Crystal Dynamics made a difficult, but necessary business decision to reduce our current studio staff by eight people," the studio said of the layoffs, first reported by Vertical Slice, in a statement provided to PC Gamer.

"Whenever we phase roles off a project, we make every effort to find new spots for our great colleagues first. Everyone affected receives a full severance package as well as job placement assistance to aid them through this transition. We wish them the best and hope to work together in the future."

The studio added that no ongoing projects are impacted by the cuts.

In terms of raw numbers, eight people is not a huge cut, especially when compared to layoffs at other studios—Firaxis reportedly cut roughly 60 employees earlier today, for instance. But it's concerning in the case of Crystal Dynamics because the studio has been bleeding for so long: This is at least the fifth round of layoffs in less than two years, and comes just eight months after the last round of cuts. Roughly 70 employees in total have been let go over that span.

The studio has also struggled to get things done with its flagship series, Tomb Raider. Crystal Dynamics regained control of the property in 2022, shortly after the studio was acquired by Embracer, but in June Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, a remake of the original game, was delayed to February 2027; less than two months later, the all-new Tomb Raider: Catalyst was pushed into 2028. The studio also co-developed the Perfect Dark reboot alongside The Initiative for four years before Microsoft killed it in July 2025.

#3594. Hillary Clinton Showed Up For Dinner at Gloria Steinem’s Townhouse

It’s a dark and stormy November night at Gloria Steinem’s townhouse, and Hillary Clinton has something to say about the 2026 election. “One of my most anticipated moments will be watching Donald Trump walk into the State of the Union through the now more than one hundred women members of the House of Representatives. I just want them all to stare at him and say, ‘You fired us from jobs we were qualified for. You insulted us. You demeaned our ambition. You undermined our place in government and society. And we’re here.’”

Huma Abedin, Busy Philips, and Paloma Elsesser.

The former Secretary of State and 2016 presidential candidate is a last-minute but highly anticipated arrival to this dinner honoring Steinem, the late activist. She passed away in September, but the feminist pathfinder was known for throwing these salon-type events (she called them “circles”) at her Upper East Side townhouse, which she bought for just $30,000 in the late ’60s. It’s overflowing with books (I spy Marilyn by Norman Mailer, Jane Fonda’s War by Mary Hershberger, and several Eleanor Roosevelt biographies on the shelves), pictures (there’s one framed of Steinem alongside Mariska Hargitay) and Indian art. (Steinem spent two formative years in the country.) There are magnets in her kitchen of Wonder Woman, Frida Kahlo, and a cloth finger puppet of Hillary Clinton. A political button is pinned to it that says “Another Bitch for Hillary.” The whole place smells like a Cire Trudon candle, and everyone’s drinking negronis. (Which actually isn’t technically very Steinem—her favorite cocktail was a margarita—but the negronis go with the night’s dinner, prepared by Lilia chef Missy Robbins.) Yet this is one of the first events at the townhouse that Steinem herself isn’t here to lead.

Jihae, Lux Pascal, Naomi Watts, and Bethann Hardison.

Amy Richards, a feminist activist whom many consider to be the daughter Steinem never had—a title Richards rejects because her mentor “didn’t want kids”—stood up at one point to tell the crowd that this is what Steinem would have wanted. Growing up with a transient father and a mentally volatile mother, the late activist took near-obsessive care in maintaining a welcoming home she could share with others. “As long as I knew Gloria, she always said, ‘I just want my home to be the way it’s always been.’ She wanted it to be filled with people,” Richards says. “She didn’t grow up with a home. She was traveling the country for the first 10 years of her life and then lived with her mother, who was not very stable.”

At least Steinem’s still here on the wall: Months before her death, she posed for a series of portraits by Paola Kudacki for Weldun, a platform that offers physically adaptive and functional fashion. It was a bit of a small miracle that Steinem said yes. “I will say, Gloria did not always love to be photographed,” Richards says. “Especially in her later years—not because of wrinkles or aging, but she was just like, ‘Aren’t there enough pictures of me?’” Weldun and the Gloria Steinem Foundation are presenting tonight’s dinner, and mementos of Steinem are everywhere. On the fireplace mantle sits a pair of her signature Ray-Ban aviators. But Gloria’s stuff isn’t the same as Gloria herself.

Former secretary of state Hillary Clinton hugging Melissa McCarthy.

Which is probably why, in a crowd of women that include Huma Abedin, Mariska Hargitay, Padma Lakshmi, Melissa McCarthy, and Bethann Hardison—who, at the ripe age of 84, shows up wearing Gucci—Clinton’s unexpected arrival feels seismic, like Gloria sent someone in her place. (Hardison tells me she thinks Steinem used whatever divine power she’s got up there to launch the Blue Wave: “She’s probably saying she helped it happen!”) Whatever your views on Clinton’s politics, she was the first woman to receive a presidential nomination from a major party. Paloma Elsesser and I sit crouched in a corner of the room, glued to the window. “There’s mother,” the supermodel whispers to me as Clinton exits her car into the pouring rain and walks up to the townhouse door.

Guests at dinner honoring the late Gloria Steinem.

“Hi, everybody,” Clinton says as she walks in. The entire dinner comes to a silent halt. “Hi,” the room responds in unison. Madame Secretary doesn’t seem to like the fuss, probably because 30 or so people intensely staring at you when you arrive at a party is objectively unsettling. “Go back to eating!” she says, motioning to the Missy Robbins meal on the table. Clinton sits down next to Naomi Watts and warmly greets Busy Philips, who stumped for Clinton back in 2016. Hargitay blows her a kiss across the table. All anyone wants to do is talk to Clinton about the 2026 election, in which Democrats won at least 55 seats in the Senate and 256 in the House to take both majorities in the US Congress. At the end of the meal—and after a proper catch-up with Shonda Rhimes—Clinton tries to leave, but she can’t. Guests block the door, clamoring to chat her up.

Amid the Clinton traffic jam, I ask Hargitay about the photo. She can’t remember exactly what it is from. “Was it Bravo? Was it with Andy…what’s his name?” But she can guess what she thinks Steinem might say about the blue wave: “There is a God!”

I watch Clinton finally make her exit. It’s late, so I wait several minutes before I descend the stairs to leave too. (I wait for Elsesser, Watts, Hardinn, and Lux Pascal to finish taking a selfie on the steps.) But I spoke too soon: Clinton’s stuck waiting for the coat check, another group of women crowded around her hoping to say something—or, more likely, hoping she says something. With the way this night is going, Clinton might be the last one at the party.

I have no idea if this is the case of some reviewers just not being in the target audience of The Hunger Games’ latest prequel Sunrise on the Reaping or if some people who have liked the other movies found this one less moving. But looking at reviews this morning after Sunrise purple carpet photos dropped, I realized not everyone felt the way I did about the 2026 movie release.

I agree with reviews on one big point: The adaptation is faithful to Suzanne Collins’ source material, which is a pretty bleak book with a bittersweet ending in the same way the third Hunger Games book is. That’s down to several scenes I personally wanted to see play out on the big screen.

Discussing Film made a big point to call out the adaptations “faithful” take on the source material. The outlet’s Yasmine Kandil wrote:

That being said, Sunrise on the Reaping remains exceedingly faithful to the novel’s sequence of events, perhaps more so than any of its predecessors, and often down to the most minute details.

In fact, I saw that word peppered in and out of reviews. If you liked the book, you should like this movie. Or as Gizmodo's Germain Lussier more than adequately puts it, if you are a fan of this franchise, you'll dig this. It's a "love letter" to fans.

Sunrise on the Reaping, is a love letter to The Hunger Games, filled with connections, explanations, and moments designed to provide maximum delight to fans of the series. It isn’t concerned with setting up the world or reexplaining the stakes. It says, 'This is the sixth movie. If you’re watching this without context, well, that’s on you.'

Still, when it comes to SOME of these reviews, I feel like I watched a completely different movie.

At Indiewire, the grade was a C- (with a bright spot in Jesse Plemons’ performance as Plutarch), and this comment from Ryan Lattanzio is really sticking with me after perusing reviews.

Sunrise on the Reaping is a dreary slog, another death-march “They Shoot Horses, Don’t They?” riff with a pretty Gen Z cast, and one that mistakes new layers of darkness (and trauma!) for the sort of profundity that its filmmakers hope will burnish a creatively withering property.

The Guardian was equally unenthusiastic about the movie, and had seemingly a lot of fun lambasting it, calling it “overwrought” and “boring,” and even making fun of the flick’s name. ( I think Peter Bradshaw’s review highlights my earlier point, that this movie isn’t for every demographic.)

Here is yet another iteration of the utterly exhausted, unbearably extended and now surreally boring Hunger Games franchise, based on the YA bestsellers by Suzanne Collins. This one has another of the series’ convoluted faux-mythic subtitles: Sunrise on the Reaping. What, “harvest dawn” not old-timey enough?

These aren’t the only two bad reviews, they are just among the more brutal and trending. (Though it's worth pointing out plenty of outlets, like THR, Time Out and more gave the film positive reviews, and it is at the time of this writing, trending positively on review aggregators.)

Honestly, is Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping perfect? No. Mckenna Grace and Jesse Plemons are standouts, and Elle Fanning and Joseph Zada do fine jobs, but I’m not bringing up Oscars here. I also think because the movie is so long, some of the emotional deaths in the arena are blunted, and I wish we had more time with characters like Maysilee, Wiress, Beetee and Ampert.

Regardless, this movie made me feel a lot of feelings about humanity, and what humans are willing to endure. Haymitch’s story ties in so hard with Katness,’ and the end cap OG Hunger Games scene where she was able to do what he could not was both hopeful and sad at the same time. This movie emotionally wrecked me. I cried multiple times. If you are a fan of the franchise at all, you should see it on the big screen. It’s proven to be a franchise with staying power and (hopefully) more stories to tell.

Jessica Rawden is Managing Editor at CinemaBlend. She’s been kicking out news stories since 2007 and joined the full-time staff in 2014. She oversees news content, hiring and training for the site, and her areas of expertise include theme parks, rom-coms, Hallmark (particularly Christmas movie season), reality TV, celebrity interviews and primetime. She loves a good animated movie. Jessica has a Masters in Library Science degree from Indiana University, and used to be found behind a reference desk most definitely not shushing people. She now uses those skills in researching and tracking down information in very different ways.
